name: SmugMug
tagline: Publish a self-hosted client gallery from user-owned photo storage
verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For SmugMug, publish a self-hosted client gallery from user-owned photo storage. The hard boundary is image hosting, global delivery, print commerce, client proofing, and support, plus image pipeline quality, models, and workflow polish.
coreLoopDIY: Catalog local photos from user-owned storage, generate previews, apply non-destructive adjustments, and publish selected images to a self-hosted client gallery.
whatYouLose: image hosting, global delivery, print commerce, client proofing, and support
moatNotes: image pipeline quality, models, and workflow polish
ongoingBurden: raw codecs, color management, metadata, previews, face models, GPU support, storage, backups, sync, and export fidelity
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for SmugMug because photographers pay because image quality, catalog safety, and fast handling of huge libraries matter more than cloning sliders. The recurring cost buys raw codecs, color management, metadata, previews, face models, GPU support, storage, backups, sync, and export fidelity, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Immich
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosted photo and video management platform.

alternatives.name: Lychee
alternatives.desc: Clean albums, passworded shares, metadata, and downloads from your own storage; no print lab, sales engine, or hand-holding.

alternatives.name: Photoview
alternatives.desc: A fast gallery over an existing folder tree with RAW, EXIF, users, share links, and downloads; minimal branding controls, maximum ownership.

alternatives.name: Piwigo
alternatives.desc: A mature self-hosted gallery with private albums, users, themes, metadata, downloads, and a huge plugin ecosystem; you become the support desk.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Immich
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Excellent backup and browsing, but client-facing gallery theming, password workflows, and presentation polish are afterthoughts.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Power plan and a personal local photo catalog DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for SmugMug in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, Rust image libraries, SQLite, and local filesystem access; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: catalog local photos from user-owned storage, generate previews, apply non-destructive adjustments, and publish selected images to a self-hosted client gallery.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Index selected folders without moving or rewriting originals and store only catalog data in SQLite.
Generate thumbnails and previews, read EXIF, detect duplicates by hash, and monitor file changes.
Provide timeline, folders, albums, ratings, flags, tags, search, and side-by-side compare.
Store edits as reversible parameters for crop, rotate, exposure, contrast, white balance, and saturation.
Render exports to a new folder with explicit color space, quality, size, and metadata choices.
Add catalog backup, missing-file repair, integrity scan, and a clear original-safety guarantee.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a proprietary raw-rendering engine.
Deliberately leave out hosted cross-device photo sync and client galleries.
Deliberately leave out frontier culling, retouching, and generative models.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
